item.text:
When you reach the foyer, Bea is seated at one of the cafe tables with a packed lunch and a closed accounts ledger. A canvas bag full of invoice folders rests against her chair. Nell joins her with a sandwich but keeps glancing towards the office.

You sit with your own lunch. Bea has put the ledger away, so you ask, “What do you enjoy about having the cinema open again?”

“Nearly open,” she says. “I’m refusing to use the present tense until the twenty-sixth. There are still too many things in boxes.”

She looks across the foyer towards the glass doors.

“I like seeing light in here. After it closed, I’d walk down Harbour Street and this whole frontage was dark. You could still see the old counter through the glass, but it looked abandoned rather than old.”

Bea unwraps half a cheese sandwich.

“I worked here four years in the eighties. It wasn’t a golden age. The foyer carpet smelt damp, the heating failed regularly and one manager used to hide broken seats by turning the lights down before anybody entered. But it was a workplace. People knew who painted the signs, who fixed the curtains and who stayed late when a screening overran.”

“That explains Rosa’s exhibition,” Nell says.

“It’s why I wanted her involved. Old things get called charming and everybody who made them disappears.”

Bea takes a bite, then continues.

“I enjoy hearing people argue about actual work again. Which cups belong where, whether the sound reaches row twelve, who has the auditorium at seven. For years the only conversation was whether the roof would finish the building off.”

“And the sign,” Nell says.

“Yes. Especially the sign.”

“You approved that restoration against your own cost recommendation.”

“I’m treasurer, not a hostage to spreadsheets.”

Nell takes another bite of her sandwich. “It was a very clear spreadsheet.”

“The sign will be visible from the harbour road. Some expenditure has a purpose beyond making the bottom line look obedient.”

Bea’s smile fades into something quieter as she glances towards the auditorium doors.

“What I’m waiting for is an ordinary week after the reopening. Not photographs, speeches or donors being shown around. A wet Saturday when children drop popcorn, somebody complains that the tea is weak, and two dozen people come because they actually want to see the film.”

She folds the sandwich wrapping neatly beneath her hand.

“My granddaughter and I send each other terrible films on secondhand discs. I want to bring her here and let her choose one without being told it’s historically important.”

The office telephone rings. Nell finishes the last bite of her sandwich and stands.

“That’ll be the crockery supplier.”

She goes to answer it, leaving you and Bea at the table while harbour traffic moves past the bright front windows.
